Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Nun
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Sister Margaret had always found solace in her faith and her work at the local convent. As a nun, she was dedicated to serving others and spreading love and kindness wherever she went. But all of that changed on the day her younger brother, John, was killed in a car accident right outside the convent's front gates. It was a typical Wednesday afternoon when Sister Margaret had been working in the garden, tending to the flowers and vegetables that the sisters grew for their own meals. She remembered hearing the screech of tires and the crunch of metal, but it wasn't until she saw her brother's car crumpled against the stone wall that reality set in. She rushed to his side, praying and crying as she tried to comfort him in his final moments. In the weeks and months that followed, Sister Margaret found herself struggling to cope with the loss of her brother. She began to avoid the front garden where the accident had occurred, taking long detours through the convent's corridors just to get from one place to another. She couldn't bear the thought of walking past the spot where her brother had died, and the sight of the stone wall now made her feel nauseous. As time went on, Sister Margaret developed a series of mental rituals that she believed would prevent similar tragedies from happening again. Every morning, she would pray for exactly 17 minutes, reciting specific prayers in a particular order, convinced that this would keep her loved ones safe. She also began to carry a small wooden cross with her at all times, touching it whenever she felt anxious or scared. Sister Margaret's memories of the accident were vivid and detailed, but they also had some disturbing gaps. She remembered the sound of the crash, the feeling of her brother's hand in hers, and the sight of his broken body. But there were moments that were completely blank, like a fog that she couldn't penetrate no matter how hard she tried. As the months turned into years, Sister Margaret became increasingly withdrawn and isolated. She stopped attending community events and avoided spending time with her fellow sisters, afraid of being reminded of her loss. Even simple tasks like cooking or cleaning became overwhelming, as every little thing seemed to trigger memories of her brother. Sister Margaret couldn't shake the feeling that she was to blame for her brother's death. If only she had been more careful, if only she had been more attentive, maybe he would still be alive. She felt like a failure, unable to protect the people she loved most in the world. And now, as she looked back on that fateful day, she couldn't help but wonder what she could have done differently. As the weight of her grief and guilt bore down on her, Sister Margaret began to doubt her own abilities. She felt like she was losing her grip on reality, unable to trust herself or her own judgment. She started to question whether she was still cut out for this life, whether she had what it took to be a nun. It was only when her superior, Mother Teresa, expressed concern about Sister Margaret's increasing isolation and withdrawal that she finally realized she needed help. With great trepidation, Sister Margaret made an appointment with a therapist, hoping against hope that someone could help her untangle the knots of grief and guilt that had taken over her life. As she sat in the waiting room, fidgeting with her wooden cross, Sister Margaret couldn't shake the feeling that she was taking a risk by seeking help. What if the therapist didn't understand? What if they judged her or told her to just "get over it"? But deep down, she knew she had no choice. She had to try and find a way out of this darkness, no matter how daunting the journey ahead might seem.
